readerTitle: Netflix waited a decade to stream. That was the plan.
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Netflix의 DVD 우편 대여 → 스트리밍 전환) + 실제 연구 (Dixit & Pindyck, 실물옵션) + 가상 적용 (물류 창고 자동화, 소프트웨어 AI 기능)
insight: 기다림은 아무것도 안 하는 것이 아니라, 되돌리기 어려운 결정을 미루면서 '나중에 고를 권리'를 사 두는 능동적인 전략이다.
misconception: 기다리는 것은 겁이 많거나 게으른 것이고, 좋은 기회는 무조건 먼저 뛰어드는 쪽이 잡는다.

sources.text: Dixit, A. K. & Pindyck, R. S. (1994). Investment under Uncertainty. Princeton University Press.
Netflix company history and press materials (DVD-by-mail service launched 1998; streaming 'Watch Instantly' launched January 2007)
Interviews with Reed Hastings on choosing the name 'Netflix' with future internet delivery in mind

factChecks.note: Netflix 설립(1997), DVD 우편 대여 시작(1998), 스트리밍 'Watch Instantly' 출시(2007년 1월)를 Netflix 공식 연혁으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 'late 1990s', '2007'로만 적었습니다.
Reed Hastings가 '처음부터 인터넷 배송을 염두에 두고 Netflix라는 이름을 골랐다'고 말한 인터뷰가 여러 매체에 있습니다. 직접 인용은 피하고 'has said'로 풀어 썼습니다. 원문 인터뷰 하나를 출처로 확정하세요.
스트리밍 출시 당시 기존 구독자에게 추가 요금 없이 제공되었다는 점을 확인하세요. 카드에는 'offered to existing subscribers'로만 적었습니다.
Dixit & Pindyck의 핵심 주장(되돌릴 수 없는 투자는 기다릴 옵션을 없애므로, 지금 투자하려면 '평균적으로 이익'보다 높은 기준을 넘어야 한다)을 단순화해 설명했습니다. 과장 없이 요약되었는지 확인하세요.
창고 자동화와 AI 기능 사례는 모두 설명용 가상 사례이며 수치가 없습니다.

cards.title: Netflix waited a decade to stream. That was the plan.
body: In the late 1990s, Netflix mailed DVDs in red envelopes. Its co-founder Reed Hastings has said the company chose the name with future internet delivery in mind.
Yet it didn't launch streaming until 2007. For years, the company it was named for didn't exist yet. The delay wasn't a failure of nerve. It was a strategy.

image.label: A red envelope with a faint play button behind it
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 우편함에 꽂힌 빨간 봉투 한 장, 그 뒤로 흐릿하게 비치는 재생 버튼 아이콘. 실제 Netflix 로고나 글자체는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Robots for your warehouse?
body: You run a regional logistics company. A vendor offers a robotic sorting system that would cut labor costs. It's expensive, hard to resell, and this kind of technology is improving fast. Two newer vendors say better models are coming.
What do you do?

options.text: Buy the full system now, before rivals do
options.feedback: You'd gain savings early, but you lock a large, hard-to-undo investment into technology that may soon look dated.

options.text: Run a small pilot on one line, and decide on the rest later
options.feedback: You learn what really works in your building while keeping most of your money and your options free. The cost is slower savings.

options.text: Hold off entirely for two years until prices fall
options.feedback: You avoid the big bet, but you also learn nothing. In two years you'll face the same decision with no more knowledge than today.

cards.title: Netflix waited, but it didn't sit still.
body: In the early 2000s, internet connections were too slow for good video at home. Building a streaming service then would have meant a costly product few people could use.
So Netflix grew the DVD business instead. It built a large base of subscribers, a habit of paying monthly, and a system for recommending titles.
When it launched streaming in 2007, it offered it to existing subscribers. The waiting years had built the audience and the know-how the new service needed.

cards.title: Waiting as a strategy
body: **Waiting as a strategy** means delaying a big, hard-to-undo commitment on purpose, so you can decide later with better information.
The key idea: the right to choose later is worth something. Once you commit, that right is gone. If the future is unclear, keeping it can be worth more than acting first.

image.label: A fork in a road with a fog bank ahead
image.brief: 갈림길 앞에 서 있는 작은 인물. 앞쪽은 안개가 끼어 있고, 인물은 지도를 펴고 쌍안경으로 안개가 걷히는 쪽을 살피는 모습. '아직 고르지 않음'이 능동적으로 보이게.

cards.title: Economists put a price on the option to wait.
body: In *Investment under Uncertainty* (1994), economists Avinash Dixit and Robert Pindyck showed why. A project that pays off on average can still be a bad bet today, because investing now kills the chance to learn first.
Waiting tends to pay when three things are true:
list: The uncertainty will **clear up with time**
You can still enter later on fair terms
cards.callout: If any one is missing, waiting loses most of its value.

cards.title: Good waiting is active waiting.
body: Smart waiters do three things while they hold off. They **watch** the signals that will settle the question, like prices, speeds or customer behavior.
They **prepare**, building the skills, customers or partners they'll need. And they set **triggers**: the conditions that will make them move.
Netflix did all three. Waiting without these is just hoping.

cards.title: Waiting has a price too.
body: Some markets reward whoever arrives first. If customers face high switching costs, or a product gets better as more people use it, a rival can lock up the market while you watch.
Waiting can also become an excuse. The fog never fully lifts. Without a deadline and clear triggers, *we're waiting for the right moment* turns into never deciding.
Ask what you'd lose if a rival moved this year, not just what you'd save.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: You run a project-management app. Customers ask for AI features. The AI tools you could build on change every few months, and prices keep shifting. One rival has already rebuilt its whole product around one AI vendor.
What's your move?

options.text: Wait a year and revisit when the tools settle down
options.feedback: You avoid a costly rebuild, but you learn nothing about what your users want. A year from now you'll still be guessing.

options.text: Ship one small AI feature, built so the vendor can be swapped, and set triggers for going bigger
options.feedback: You learn from real usage and keep customers happy, without locking into tools that may change. The cost is a less flashy launch than your rival's.

options.text: Match the rival and rebuild everything around one AI vendor
options.feedback: You'd look modern fast, but you'd make a hard-to-undo bet on tools that change every few months.

cards.title: Waiting is a choice, not a lack of one.
body: When a commitment is hard to undo and the future is unclear, the right to decide later is worth protecting. Use the time to watch, prepare and set triggers.
**Try it today:** pick one big decision you're putting off. Write down what you're waiting to learn, what would make you move, and the date you'll decide either way.
